title: Primary immunodeficiencies: cases
covers: Five teaching cases that link a clinical picture to its diagnosis: chronic granulomatous disease, Wiskott-Aldrich, Chediak-Higashi, X-linked SCID and hyper-IgE syndrome.

items.p: Each case has one clue that points to the diagnosis. Learn the clue, the confirming test and the gene.

table: Aspergillus pneumonia, normal blood count and antibodies
Eczema, infections, few and small platelets
Pale skin and hair, infections, giant granules
Infections from 3 months, no T cells, B cells present
Cold staphylococcal abscesses, fractures, huge IgE

items.p: A teenage gardener nearly dies of Aspergillus pneumonia. Blood count and immunoglobulins are normal, so the defect is in phagocyte killing.
His neutrophils do not reduce DHR, and neither do his brother's. His mother and sister each have two populations of cells: they are carriers. The disease is X-linked.
A boy with eczema, recurrent infections, bloody diarrhea and petechiae. His platelets are very few and abnormally small. Later he develops autoimmune hemolytic anemia (positive Coombs test).

ul: Antibodies: normal IgG, low IgM, high IgA and IgE; poor vaccine responses
Gene: WAS, X-linked. The protein WASP is found in white cells and megakaryocytes, which explains both problems.
A rare recessive form is caused by WIPF1

items.note: The slide gives a later platelet count of "150000 per uL" while describing platelets as still low. That value is within the normal range; it is probably a typing error.

items.p: A girl of related parents with ear and lung infections, easy bruising, sensitivity to light, and skin and hair lighter than her family. Antibodies, complement and DHR are normal. The smear shows giant granules in white cells.

ul: Autosomal recessive; gene LYST, needed for vesicle trafficking
Neutrophils migrate poorly; NK and cytotoxic T cells kill poorly
Partial albinism: melanocytes cannot hand over their melanosomes
Later: progressive neurological disease, and an accelerated phase with lymphocyte infiltration and pancytopenia

items.p: A boy who was well at birth. From 3 months: cough, ear infections, pneumonia, thrush, poor growth. He has very few lymphocytes, no CD3 cells, normal B cells and few NK cells: X-linked SCID.

A boy with eczema from the first month, repeated staphylococcal skin infections that are not red, hot or painful, pneumonias, fractures after minor injury, a prominent forehead and a wide nose. IgE is enormously raised, with eosinophilia.

ul: Triad: staphylococcal skin abscesses, pneumonia, very high IgE
Also Candida infections; little fever or inflammation
Most common form: autosomal dominant STAT3 mutation (dominant negative), with bone and dental features
Recessive forms (for example DOCK8) have no skeletal features
IL-17 normally recruits phagocytes and drives defensin production in skin

cards.q: Severe Aspergillus infection with normal blood count and immunoglobulins: think of...
cards.a: Chronic granulomatous disease; confirm with the DHR test

cards.q: DHR test: two populations of neutrophils in a mother means...
cards.a: She is a carrier of X-linked chronic granulomatous disease.
Eczema, recurrent infections, thrombocytopenia with small platelets
Normal IgG, low IgM, high IgA and IgE
WAS (protein WASP, in white cells and megakaryocytes); X-linked recessive
Recurrent bacterial infections, partial oculocutaneous albinism, bleeding tendency; later neurological decline
Giant cytoplasmic granules in leukocytes; LYST (vesicle trafficking); autosomal recessive

cards.q: Why is the skin pale in Chediak-Higashi?
cards.a: Melanocytes cannot transfer melanosomes to keratinocytes.

cards.q: Boy with no CD3 cells, normal B cells, low NK cells

cards.a: Staphylococcal skin abscesses ("cold"), pneumonia, very high IgE

cards.q: Hyper-IgE syndrome: most frequent gene and extra features
cards.a: STAT3, autosomal dominant (dominant negative); bone fragility and dental anomalies

cards.q: Why are abscesses "cold" in hyper-IgE syndrome?
cards.a: Patients do not mount strong inflammatory responses (no redness, warmth or fever).

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy working with a gardening crew develops respiratory failure. Imaging shows large cotton-ball densities in both lungs; needle aspiration grows Aspergillus fumigatus. CBC and immunoglobulins are normal. Which test is most appropriate next?

options.B: Lymphocyte subset count for CD3 cells

questions.explanation: Severe Aspergillus infection with normal CBC and immunoglobulins suggests chronic granulomatous disease; the DHR test was performed in the patient and his family. B: CBC is normal and the fungal lung infection points to a phagocyte defect. C: That is the clue for Chediak-Higashi syndrome. D: That is the clue for hyper-IgE syndrome. E: That is the clue for Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.

questions.stem: In the family of that patient, he and his brother do not reduce DHR, while his mother and sister each show two populations of cells. What does this pattern indicate?

options.A: Autosomal recessive CGD, with both parents as carriers
options.B: Autosomal dominant CGD, with variable expression in females
options.C: X-linked CGD, with the mother and sister affected
options.D: Myeloperoxidase deficiency in the whole family
options.E: X-linked CGD, with the mother and sister as carriers

questions.explanation: The patient and his brother did not reduce DHR; mother and sister had two populations of cells (carriers). Diagnosis: X-linked CGD, to be confirmed by sequencing. The brother had had a perirectal abscess in infancy. A: Two cell populations in the females indicate X-linked carriers. B: Not the interpretation. C: They are carriers with a mixed population. D: The DHR pattern points to X-linked CGD.

questions.stem: A 20-month-old boy has eczema since 6 months, recurrent ear and respiratory infections, bloody diarrhea and petechiae. Platelet count is 10,000/µL and platelets are abnormally small. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.explanation: Recurrent infections, eczema, bloody diarrhea and severe thrombocytopenia with abnormally small platelets in a male infant: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. A: Eczema and infections occur, but small platelets with thrombocytopenia point elsewhere. B: That shows albinism and giant granules. C: No thrombocytopenia or eczema. E: No thrombocytopenia or eczema.

questions.stem: At 18 months the same child becomes pale with dark urine; hemoglobin is 5 g/dL and the direct Coombs test is positive. Which complication of his disease is this?

options.A: Anemia from chronic blood loss in stool

questions.explanation: A positive direct Coombs test demonstrated autoimmune hemolytic anemia, treated with steroids. A: The positive Coombs test shows antibody-mediated hemolysis. C: Not the complication described. D: Not shown. E: He is 18 months old.

questions.stem: Which immunological profile was found in the child with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome?

options.A: Low IgG, high IgM, low IgA and low IgE
options.B: Normal IgG, high IgM, low IgA and normal IgE
options.C: Normal IgG, low IgM, high IgA and high IgE
options.E: Normal IgG, normal IgM, normal IgA and very high IgE

questions.explanation: Normal IgG, low IgM, high IgA and high IgE, with poor antibody response to conjugated polysaccharide vaccines, normal numbers of B and T cells and abnormal in-vitro T-cell proliferation. A: That resembles hyper-IgM syndrome. B: Not the profile shown. D: That resembles XLA. E: That resembles hyper-IgE syndrome.

questions.stem: Why does a WAS mutation cause both immunodeficiency and thrombocytopenia?

options.A: WASP is expressed in endothelial cells and hepatocytes
options.B: WASP is a platelet surface receptor for von Willebrand factor
options.C: WASP is required for V(D)J recombination in lymphocytes and megakaryocytes
options.D: WASP is a complement regulator on platelets
options.E: WASP is expressed in white blood cells and megakaryocytes

questions.explanation: Gene WAS (Xp11.23), X-linked recessive. The protein WASP is expressed in white blood cells and megakaryocytes, hence immunodeficiency and thrombocytopenia. The patient received HSCT. A: Not the cells named. B: Not its described role. C: Not its described role. D: Not its described role.

questions.stem: Besides the X-linked WAS form, which gene causes an autosomal recessive form of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome?

options.A: LYST, encoding a vesicle trafficking protein
options.C: STAT3, with a dominant negative effect

questions.explanation: Another gene involved is WIPF1 (WIP), encoding WASP-interacting protein: the AR form. A: That is Chediak-Higashi syndrome. C: That is hyper-IgE syndrome. D: That is X-linked SCID. E: That is XLA.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl of consanguineous parents has recurrent ear infections, pneumonia, easy bruising, photophobia, and skin and hair much lighter than her family. Immunoglobulins, complement and DHR are normal. Which finding on the blood smear clinches the diagnosis?

options.A: Abnormally small platelets with a low count

questions.explanation: Peripheral smear showed giant cytoplasmic granules in her leukocytes, positive for myeloperoxidase: Chediak-Higashi syndrome. Labs: mild neutropenia, normal Ig, complement and DHR. A: That is Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. B: Lymphocyte numbers were normal. C: Not the finding. E: That fits hyper-IgE syndrome.

options.A: Recurrent bacterial infections, eczema and small platelets
options.B: Skin abscesses, pneumonia and very high IgE
options.C: Bacterial infections, oculocutaneous albinism and bleeding
options.D: Recurrent fungal infections, granulomas and abnormal DHR
options.E: Recurrent viral infections, absent T cells and failure to thrive

questions.explanation: CHS is a very rare, severe autosomal recessive disease with recurrent bacterial infections, partial oculocutaneous albinism and a bleeding tendency due to (mild to moderate) platelet dysfunction. A: That is Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. B: That is hyper-IgE syndrome. D: That is CGD. E: That is SCID.

questions.stem: The girl with Chediak-Higashi syndrome received a bone marrow transplant. What happened in adolescence, as is typical of the disease?

options.B: Recurrence of pyogenic infections with loss of the graft
options.C: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia with positive Coombs test

questions.explanation: Years later she developed a progressive neurological disease (weakness, tremors, ataxia). Most patients who survive into adolescence develop neurological defects: cerebellar ataxia, CNS atrophy, seizures, peripheral neuropathy, cognitive defects. B: The course described is neurological. C: That was the Wiskott-Aldrich case. D: That belongs to hyper-IgE syndrome. E: That was the CGD case.

questions.stem: What is the "accelerated" complication that most patients with Chediak-Higashi syndrome undergo at some point?

options.A: Uncontrolled eosinophil proliferation with very high IgE
options.B: Loss of germinal centers with hypogammaglobulinemia

questions.explanation: Most patients undergo uncontrolled lymphocyte proliferation and lymphohistiocytic infiltration, with fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and pancytopenia. A: Not CHS. B: Not CHS. C: Not CHS. D: Not CHS.

questions.stem: Which gene is mutated in Chediak-Higashi syndrome, and what is its function?

options.B: WAS; actin regulation in megakaryocytes and white cells

questions.explanation: Gene CHS1 or LYST, involved in vesicle formation and trafficking; abnormal trafficking may cause aberrant vesicle fusion and failure to transport lysosomes to the right location. A: That is the CGD mechanism. B: That is Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. D: That is FMF. E: That is hyper-IgE syndrome.

questions.stem: Which immune defects are described in Chediak-Higashi syndrome?

options.A: Absent respiratory burst in neutrophils; normal cytotoxicity of NK cells
options.B: Reduced chemotactic capacity of neutrophils; impaired NK cytotoxicity
options.C: Absent B cells; normal chemotaxis of neutrophils
options.D: Absent T cells; normal NK cells

questions.explanation: Affected neutrophils and monocytes have decreased chemotactic and migratory capacity; cytotoxic T cells and NK cells have severely impaired cytotoxicity: a defect of innate immunity against pyogenic infections. A: The burst (DHR) is normal and cytotoxicity is impaired. C: B cells are not the problem. D: Lymphocyte numbers are normal. E: Complement titers were normal.

questions.stem: Why do patients with Chediak-Higashi syndrome have light skin and hair?

options.B: Melanocytes are absent from the skin
options.C: Tyrosinase is deficient, so melanin is not made

questions.explanation: The pigmentation defect is due to the inability of melanocytes to transfer melanosomes (pigment-containing granules) to keratinocytes and other epithelial cells. B: Melanocytes are present; transfer fails. C: Not the mechanism given. D: Not the mechanism given. E: Not the mechanism given.

questions.stem: A boy, normal at birth, has cough from 3 months, recurrent otitis, bilateral pneumonia, oral thrush and failure to thrive. Lymphocytes are 760/µL with no CD3 cells, a normal B-cell count and a low NK-cell count. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.explanation: No CD3 cells, normal B cells and low NK cells (T−B+NK−) in a boy, with decreased IgG and IgA: γ chain deficiency. A: B cells would be absent and NK cells present. B: B cells would be absent as well. C: NK cells would be normal. E: T cells would be normal and B cells absent.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy has had severe eczema since the first month, recurrent Staphylococcus aureus skin infections without redness, pain or warmth, two pneumonias, two fractures after minor trauma, a prominent forehead and a wide nasal bridge. Which laboratory result is expected?

options.D: High IgM with low IgG and IgA

questions.explanation: Labs: hypereosinophilia (7%), IgE 36,698 (normal 0–200), IgG and IgA normal, IgM slightly high; sequencing showed a heterozygous STAT3 mutation: hyper-IgE syndrome with cold abscesses and bone fragility. A: That is Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. C: That is CGD. D: That is hyper-IgM syndrome. E: That is Chediak-Higashi syndrome.

questions.stem: Which triad defines hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome, and to which organisms are patients susceptible?

options.A: Staphylococcal abscesses, pneumonia, high IgE; S. aureus and Candida
options.B: Eczema, thrombocytopenia and infections; encapsulated bacteria
options.C: Albinism, bleeding and infections; pyogenic bacteria
options.D: Staphylococcal skin abscesses, meningitis and low IgE; Neisseria
options.E: Granulomas, abscesses and fungal pneumonia; Aspergillus

questions.explanation: HIES triad: recurrent staphylococcal skin abscesses, pneumonia and very high serum IgE. Susceptibility to Staph aureus and Candida albicans. Abscesses lack warmth and redness; patients do not mount strong inflammatory responses such as fever. Diagnosis uses an NIH score. B: That is Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. C: That is Chediak-Higashi syndrome. D: IgE is very high and pneumonia is part of the triad. E: That is CGD.

questions.stem: Which statement about the genetics of hyper-IgE syndrome is correct?

options.A: The autosomal recessive STAT3 form is the most frequent and spares the skeleton
options.B: The autosomal dominant DOCK8 form is the most frequent and includes skeletal features
options.C: The X-linked STAT3 form affects boys and spares the teeth
options.D: The autosomal dominant STAT3 form is a gain of function limited to the skin
options.E: The autosomal dominant STAT3 form (dominant negative) is the most frequent

questions.explanation: The AD form is the most frequent (familial or sporadic): STAT3 with a dominant negative effect; multisystemic presentation with immune defects, bone fragility and dental anomalies. AR forms (such as DOCK8 deficiency) lack skeletal manifestations. A: The STAT3 form is autosomal dominant with bone fragility. B: DOCK8 deficiency is an AR form without skeletal manifestations. C: STAT3 HIES is autosomal dominant with dental anomalies. D: The effect is dominant negative and multisystemic.

questions.stem: Why does impaired IL-17 function contribute to skin and mucosal infections in hyper-IgE syndrome?

options.A: IL-17 drives class switching to IgE and eosinophil survival
options.B: IL-17 activates macrophages to kill intracellular microbes
options.C: IL-17 induces germinal centers and affinity maturation
options.D: IL-17 recruits phagocytes and promotes defensin production
options.E: IL-17 inhibits neutrophil migration to limit abscesses

questions.explanation: IL-17 is important for mucosal and epithelial immunity, for recruiting phagocytic cells to the site of infection, and for defensin production (skin immunity). A: Those are IL-4 and IL-5 functions. B: That is the IFN-γ role. C: That is the Tfh/IL-21 role. E: IL-17 recruits phagocytic cells.
